title: Jason, Menelaus and the Murder of Onias
sum: With Heliodorus gone, Simon the temple officer turns on Onias, and Onias goes to the king. But Seleucus IV dies, and under the new king, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, Onias's brother Jason buys the high priesthood. For more money he gets leave to found a gymnasium and an ephebate and to enroll "the Antiochenes in Jerusalem." The writer calls it "the height of the Greek way": priests leave the altar for the games, and Jason sends money to Tyre for a sacrifice to Heracles, though his envoys refuse to use it so.

Three years later Jason's own messenger Menelaus, Simon's brother, outbids him and takes the office "with the fury of a wild beast." To pay, Menelaus steals temple vessels. When Onias exposes him from the sanctuary at Daphne, Menelaus has the king's deputy Andronicus lure him out and kill him; the king, grieved, executes Andronicus. In Jerusalem the people kill Menelaus's brother Lysimachus for robbing the temple, but when the elders bring their case to the king, Menelaus bribes his way free and the elders are put to death. The writer's lesson runs through it all: "it is no light thing to be ungodly toward the divine laws" (4:17).
readings: This chapter is the fullest ancient account of the Jerusalem high priests from 175 to about 170 BC. Historians test it against Josephus, who tells the story differently, and against what is known of Greek civic life. Most accept its outline: an office sold to the highest bidder, a Greek civic body founded in Jerusalem, the murder of Onias III.

The writer arranges events so that each villain is paid in his own coin. Jason cheats his brother and is cheated; Andronicus dies where he killed; Lysimachus, the temple robber, dies by the treasury. The pattern teaches the readers that God's justice works in history, even through pagan kings.

views.C: Catholic readers take the chapter as part of an inspired book and draw from it a lesson about the priesthood: an office from God cannot be bought, and holiness of life matters more than rank. Onias is the model priest, and the book will show him in glory praying for his people (15:12–14). On the canon question, see the card on the book page.
views.O: The Orthodox read 2 Maccabees in the Septuagint Old Testament and hear in this chapter the background of the martyrs they honor on 1 August. Onias the righteous high priest, "zealous for the laws" (4:2), is set against the Greek-minded rulers, as the faithful against the world.
views.P: Protestants who do not count the book as Scripture still find here the best account of the events Daniel 11:21–24 describes in veiled form, and the background of the gymnasium of 1 Maccabees 1:14. Luther's preface said 2 Maccabees was less valuable than 1 Maccabees but still useful reading.
views.H: Historians value this chapter more than almost any other in the book. The sale of the high priesthood, the founding of a Greek civic body and the murder of Onias fit what is known of Seleucid finance and Greek cities. Scholars debate what "the Antiochenes in Jerusalem" were (Bickerman, Tcherikover) and whether Onias's murder is the real reason for Andronicus's death, which Diodorus links to another killing.
views.J: The rabbis do not tell this story, but they remember the struggle with Hellenizers. The Mishnah says the priestly family of Bilgah was punished at the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 5:8), and the Tosefta explains it by a Miriam of that house who went over to the Greek rulers; some scholars link the name Bilgah to Menelaus (see the note on 4:23).

deep.h: Two stories of the high priests
deep.b:
2 Maccabees and Josephus tell different stories. In 2 Maccabees, Onias III is alive when his brother Jason buys the office (4:7), Menelaus is the brother of Simon the temple officer (4:23), and Onias is murdered near Antioch about 170 BC (4:34). In Josephus, Jason ("Jesus") succeeds after Onias has died, Menelaus is a third brother also called Onias, and the Tobiad family backs Menelaus (Antiquities 12.237–240). Elsewhere Josephus says Onias's son fled to Egypt and built a temple there (Antiquities 13.62–73), while the Jewish War gives the founding to Onias himself (Jewish War 1.31–33).

Most historians prefer 2 Maccabees, which is earlier and closer to Jerusalem. Its account of Onias's murder is also supported, at least in part, by Diodorus, who knew of an Andronicus executed for a murder (Diodorus 30.7.2). Whichever account is right, both agree that the high priesthood had become something kings sold and rivals fought over.

To Jason and his supporters the gymnasium was the door to the wider world. A Greek city with an ephebate could send envoys to festivals (4:18–19), win the king's favor and give its young men the education that opened careers across the Hellenistic world. Jason did not touch the temple worship; his envoys could still refuse to fund a sacrifice to Heracles (4:19–20).

To the writer it was the start of apostasy. He coins "the Greek way" (Hellēnismos, 4:13) as the opposite of "Judaism" (2:21), and shows priests running from the altar to the wrestling school. 1 Maccabees adds that young men undid their circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:15). Historians since Tcherikover and Hengel have shown how much Greek culture had already entered Judea, and that the conflict was among Jews before it was between Jews and the king. The writer himself wrote polished Greek: his quarrel is not with the language, but with letting another people's way of life replace the law.

echoes: Daniel 9:26; Daniel 11:21–24; 1 Maccabees 1:11–15; 1 Maccabees 7:9; 1 Kings 2:35; Ezekiel 44:15; Psalm 7:15–16; Isaiah 10:5; Romans 2:22; 1 Corinthians 7:18; Galatians 1:13–14

settings.to: the king's men and the public
settings.when: soon after Heliodorus's failure (chapter 3), about 175 BC
settings.why: To turn the blame for Heliodorus's flogging on Onias and to paint the high priest as a plotter, so that the king would remove him.
settings.readers: The book's readers lived under high priests who were not of Onias's family: Jonathan and Simon were made high priests by a king's letter and a popular decree (1 Maccabees 10:20; 1 Maccabees 14:41). Many scholars think the praise of Onias here, and his place in the dream of 15:12–14, speak to readers who knew the old line had lost the office.
views: Most commentators accept the writer's picture: Onias was the last high priest of the old line to serve as the law required, and Simon's charge was false.
Others note that the book tells only one side. Josephus says nothing of Simon's slander, and the quarrel may have been about money and power as much as about piety.

settings.to: Antiochus IV, in a private meeting
settings.why: To buy the high priesthood and the right to found a gymnasium and a body of "Antiochenes," turning Jerusalem toward a Greek city under his own control.
settings.readers: The letters at the head of the book are to Jews in Egypt (1:1, 10). Josephus says Onias's son founded a rival temple in Egypt at Leontopolis (Antiquities 13.62–73), so readers there knew the family well, and knew that a high priest's line could be broken by politics.
views: Bickerman and Hengel read the offer as a real reform program: Jason wanted Jerusalem to share in the Greek world, as other cities of the region were doing.
The writer, and many readers since, see only a bribe: a high priest who paid for God's office and then sold his people's way of life.

settings.what: The writer's verdict on the reform
settings.by: the summarizer of Jason of Cyrene (2:23)
settings.when: written between about 124 and 63 BC, looking back
settings.why: To name what Jason did, "the Greek way," as apostasy, and to warn that ungodliness toward the laws brings its own punishment.
settings.readers: The readers kept the law in Greek cities, where the gymnasium was the road to citizenship and a career. 3 Maccabees, a Greek Jewish book probably from Egypt, tells of Jews pressed to be enrolled through the rites of Dionysus (3 Maccabees 2:28–30). This verdict told such readers that no civic honor was worth the law.
views: Many scholars think the writer had his own readers in mind: Jews tempted to trade the law for Greek honors.
Others note that the writer says nothing against Greek learning as such, only against giving up the law and the temple service for it.

settings.by: the Jews of Antioch, with Greeks joining them
settings.why: To protest the murder of Onias, killed after a sworn pledge in a place of sanctuary, and to ask for justice.
settings.readers: Readers in Greek cities knew that Jews could appeal to a king and win; the book will later give royal letters that restore their rights (11:22–33). The scene, Greeks and Jews united against injustice, showed such readers that the law and Greek decency need not be enemies.
views: Many accept that the king did execute Andronicus and that Onias's death caused an outcry.
Others, noting Diodorus 30.7.2, think the king had his own reasons for putting Andronicus to death and the writer has given it a pious meaning.

settings.by: three men sent by the council of elders
settings.why: To accuse Menelaus of the temple thefts and the riot that followed, and to ask the king to remove him.
settings.readers: Antiochus III's charter had named the Jewish council (Josephus, Antiquities 12.142), and 2 Maccabees speaks of it again (1:10; 11:27). Readers who lived under a council and a high priest would see what happened when a high priest bought the king's favor against his own people.
views: The writer presents the three men as innocent victims, honored even by Tyre.
Historians see an ordinary court intrigue: Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, later a governor (8:8), was the man to bribe.

title: The Temple Plundered
sum: As Antiochus prepares his second invasion of Egypt, Jerusalem sees armies charging in the sky for forty days. A false report of the king's death brings Jason back with a thousand men; he slaughters his own people but fails, and dies an exile among the Spartans, unburied. The king takes the attack for a revolt of Judea, storms the city and kills or sells tens of thousands. Guided by Menelaus, he goes into the temple and carries off its vessels and 1,800 talents.

The writer stops to explain. The Lord was angry "for a short while" over the people's sins, so the temple was not protected as it had been against Heliodorus: "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19). The king leaves cruel governors behind, and Apollonius, the commander of the Mysians, takes the city by a trick on the Sabbath. Judas Maccabeus withdraws with about nine others to the mountains, living on plants rather than eat what defiles.
readings: The chapter tells of Jason's coup and the king's attack, which 1 Maccabees does not mention, and puts the robbing of the temple after the second Egyptian war, where 1 Maccabees 1:20 puts it after the first. Historians use the chapter to ask why the persecution began.

The center is the writer's reflection (5:17–20): the temple's fate depends on the people's faithfulness. The holy place is not magic. God chose it for his people, and when they sin, it suffers with them; when he is reconciled, it rises with them.

views.C: Catholic readers see in 5:17–20 an inspired teaching about God's ways with his people: punishment for sin is short and corrective, and his mercy restores. The saying that God chose the place for the nation is read alongside Jesus' words that real worshipers "will worship the Father in spirit and truth" (John 4:23).
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in the sack of the temple the suffering that prepared the martyrdoms of chapters 6–7. The temple is holy, but its holiness depends on the faithfulness of those who worship there.
views.P: Protestants value the chapter's history and its theology of the temple, while not taking it as Scripture. The saying of 5:19 agrees with the prophets, such as Jeremiah's warning not to trust in "the temple of the LORD" (Jeremiah 7:4).
views.H: Historians use the chapter for Jason's coup, which only this book reports, and for the theory that the persecution answered a revolt (Tcherikover). They doubt its numbers (80,000 in three days) and note that its order of events differs from 1 Maccabees and from Daniel 11:28–30.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers the defilement of the temple more than the details of this chapter. The rabbis held that the Sabbath may be broken to save life (Talmud, Yoma 85a–b), the lesson Mattathias had drawn in 1 Maccabees 2:39–41 after such Sabbath attacks as 5:25–26.

deep.h: Why did God protect the temple once and not again?
deep.b:
Chapter 3 showed God guarding the treasury: heavenly riders struck down Heliodorus (3:24–30). Now Antiochus walks in and robs it. The writer's answer is that the people had sinned (5:17–18). The temple is holy, but it is holy for the people's sake: "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19). So when the people are punished, the place shares their disaster, and when God is reconciled to them, it shares their glory (5:20), as it will when Judas rededicates it (10:1–8).

The prophets had said the same of Solomon's temple (Jeremiah 7:1–15; Ezekiel 10). Jesus warned that the second temple too would fall (Mark 13:2). After AD 70 Jews and Christians alike had to explain how God could let his house be destroyed, and the answer of this chapter, that the people matter more than the place, served both.

1 Maccabees puts the robbing of the temple in 169 BC, after Antiochus's first campaign in Egypt (1 Maccabees 1:20–24), and a massacre two years later by a tribute officer (1 Maccabees 1:29–35). 2 Maccabees puts the robbing "about this time" as the king prepared his second campaign (5:1), after Jason's coup, and then sends Apollonius (5:24–26). Josephus has two visits, in the years 143 and 145 (Antiquities 12.246–250). Daniel 11:28–30 can be read as two returns from Egypt as well. Many historians think the king came twice, robbing the temple in 169 and punishing the city in 168, and that 2 Maccabees has joined the two. Others prefer the book's order. The sky armies of 5:2–4 belong to the writer's way of marking turning points.

echoes: Daniel 11:28–30; 1 Maccabees 1:20–40; 1 Maccabees 2:29–41; Jeremiah 7:4–14; Jeremiah 22:18–19; Isaiah 14:13–20; Isaiah 54:7–8; Psalm 79:1–3; 2 Kings 6:17; Hebrews 11:38; John 11:48

settings.when: 168 BC, as the sky armies were seen
settings.why: To ask that the omen of armies in the sky would mean good and not disaster.
settings.readers: The book was read by Jews who knew how the story ended: the temple was robbed, then purified (10:1–8). Josephus shows that such omens were still reported and argued over before the fall of the second temple (Jewish War 6.297–299). The prayer teaches readers to meet signs with prayer.
views: Some think the writer passes on a story of an omen told in Jerusalem at the time.
Many note that the writer uses heavenly appearances at turning points (3:25; 10:29; 11:8) and that this one marks the start of disaster.

settings.why: To answer why God let Antiochus rob the temple when he had protected it from Heliodorus: the people had sinned, and God's anger was short.
settings.readers: The book was sent to Jews of Egypt to urge them to keep the feast of the temple's purification (1:9, 18). Readers far from Jerusalem, some of whom had a temple of their own at Leontopolis (Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73), are told that the Jerusalem temple's worth lies in the people God chose.
views: Schwartz argues that the writer, a Diaspora Jew in his view, puts the people above the temple, so that Jews outside Judea need not feel second-class.
Doran and others stress that the book still centers on the temple and its feasts; the reflection defends its holiness by explaining its fall.

title: The Decree and the Death of Eleazar
sum: The king sends an elderly Athenian to force the Jews off their ancestral laws. The temple in Jerusalem is renamed for Olympian Zeus, the one on Gerizim for Zeus, Protector of Guests. Gentiles revel and lie with women in the holy courts, forbidden sacrifices load the altar, and no one may keep the Sabbath or the feasts or even say "I am a Jew." Jews are forced to eat at the king's monthly birthday sacrifice and to march for Dionysus. Two mothers who circumcised their babies are thrown from the wall with the infants, and Sabbath-keepers hidden in caves are burned.

The writer turns to his readers: these punishments are meant for correction, not ruin. God lets other nations' sins reach their full measure before he judges them, but disciplines his own people early, and never leaves them (6:12–17). Then he tells of Eleazar, a scribe of ninety. Forced to eat pork, he spits it out. Old friends offer to let him eat permitted meat and pretend; he refuses, so as not to lead the young astray, and dies under the blows, "in my soul I suffer this with joy" (6:30), leaving his death as an example to the nation.
readings: The decree and its cruelties match 1 Maccabees 1:41–64 and Josephus. Historians debate who designed the new cult and why the king, whose empire held many religions, tried to abolish this one.

Eleazar's death is the first of the martyr stories, told so that readers might copy it. The scene is built on speeches: the friends' offer, his reasoned refusal, his dying words. Later Jewish and Christian martyr stories follow its pattern.

views.C: Catholic readers honor Eleazar among the Holy Maccabean Martyrs, kept in the Roman Martyrology on 1 August, and read 6:12–17 as inspired teaching that God's punishments are medicine for his people. His refusal to pretend has been held up to clergy and the old as a model of integrity.
views.O: The Orthodox churches keep the Holy Maccabees, Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, on 1 August, at the start of the fast before the Dormition. Gregory of Nazianzus preached that they deserved honor though their martyrdom came before Christ (Oration 15).
views.P: Protestants do not take the book as Scripture but have long admired Eleazar's refusal to pretend. The teaching that God disciplines those he loves agrees with Proverbs 3:11–12 and Hebrews 12:5–11, and many think Hebrews 11:35 has Eleazar's torture frame in view.
views.H: Historians accept the persecution as real and the renaming of the temple as likely. They see the reflection of 6:12–17 as the summarizer's own, and Eleazar's story as shaped by the forms of Greek noble-death accounts, whether or not a real scribe lies behind it.
views.J: The Talmud does not tell of Eleazar. It reports a ruling that in a time of royal decree a Jew must give up his life rather than break even a minor custom, while in ordinary times only the gravest sins, or a public act, demand it (Bavli Sanhedrin 74a–b). The rabbis also taught that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Bavli Yoma 85a–b), against the choice of the cave martyrs of 6:11.

deep.b:
Why does God let his own people suffer while the nations prosper? The writer's answer (6:12–17) is that God's quick punishment of Israel is a kindness. With the other nations he waits until their sins are full and then judges them once and for all, as he waited until "the guilt of the Amorites" was full (Genesis 15:16). With Israel he acts at once, so that its sins never pile up to the point of destruction. "He trains his own people by misfortune, yet he never leaves them" (6:16).

The idea is old in Israel: "The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject" (Proverbs 3:11). Wisdom of Solomon says much the same: God "scourges our enemies ten thousand times more" when he disciplines his own (Wisdom 12:22). Hebrews applies it to Christians who suffer (Hebrews 12:5–11). Job is the great warning against applying it too quickly to a sufferer's face. On how Christians answer the question, see the card at Job 5.

deep.h: Eleazar and the question of pretending
deep.b:
Eleazar could have saved his life with a harmless trick: eat meat he was allowed, and let people think it was the sacrifice (6:21). He refuses for a reason that looks outward. The young would think he had gone over to foreign ways (6:24–25), and his example would lead them astray. His dignity, his age and the law all point the same way (6:23).

The question came back in every persecution. In the third century, Christians who bought certificates saying they had sacrificed, without sacrificing, were counted among the lapsed and had to do penance (Cyprian, On the Lapsed). In the sixteenth century Calvin wrote against Protestants in France who went to Mass while believing otherwise, calling them "Nicodemites." Rabbinic law, too, distinguishes between private and public acts under persecution. Eleazar's answer, that a teacher's public act teaches, is the one most traditions have honored.

echoes: Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; 1 Maccabees 1:41–64; 1 Maccabees 2:29–41; Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 11:7–8; Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 11:35; Hebrews 12:5–11; Matthew 10:28; Matthew 23:32; 1 Corinthians 8:13

settings.by: Antiochus IV, through "an elderly Athenian" and the governors
settings.to: the Jews of Judea and Samaria, and then of the nearby Greek cities
settings.why: To end the Jews' life under their ancestral laws, rename the temples for Zeus and force Jews to take part in the king's sacrifices and festivals.
settings.readers: Readers in Egypt lived under Ptolemaic kings who also promoted the cult of Dionysus. 3 Maccabees, a Greek Jewish book probably from Egypt, tells of Ptolemy IV ordering Jews to be registered and branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus (3 Maccabees 2:28–30). The decree of 6:1–9 showed them where such pressure could lead.
views: 1 Maccabees 1:41 makes it the king's own order for all his kingdom to be one people.
Bickerman argued that Menelaus and his party designed the new cult, and the king backed them; 2 Maccabees' blame of Menelaus (5:15, 23; 13:4) fits that view.

settings.what: The writer's appeal to his readers
settings.why: To keep the readers from losing heart at the martyr stories to come, by explaining suffering as God's discipline of a people he does not abandon.
settings.readers: The book was first read by Jews who knew the persecution had ended and the temple was restored (10:1–8). The first letter urges them to keep the feast of that restoration (1:9). The appeal reads their own history, and any hardship of their own, as discipline that ends in mercy.
views: Most scholars see here the writer's key to the whole book: sin, punishment, the martyrs' deaths, and then God's mercy (7:38; 8:5).
Others stress that the appeal is meant to comfort, not to explain every suffering, which is why the writer keeps it short (6:17).

settings.by: the men in charge of the sacrifice, old friends of Eleazar
settings.why: To save their friend's life by a pretense: let him eat meat he was allowed while they reported that he had eaten the sacrifice.
settings.readers: Readers living as a minority among Greeks often faced pressure to make small outward gestures. The writer's answer, through Eleazar, is that a teacher's private trick becomes a public lesson. Josephus shows Jews of the Greek cities defending their right to keep their customs before Roman officials (Antiquities 12.125–126), so the question was alive for them.
views: The friends mean well; the writer says they acted out of old friendship (6:22).
Many readers see the offer as the subtler test: not force, but an easy way out.

settings.to: the officials, and the young who would hear of it
settings.why: To refuse the pretense, explain that it would lead the young astray and shame his age, and choose to die as an example.
settings.readers: The book was meant to be read for "benefit" (2:25), and here it says so: Eleazar dies to leave "a fine pattern" for the young (6:28). For readers among Greeks, the speech uses the Greek ideal of a noble death to argue for keeping the law.
views: Some think the speech preserves the memory of a real scribe's death.
Most think the writer composed it, as Greek historians composed speeches, to show what such a man would say.

settings.to: the Lord, and those standing by
settings.why: To declare before God that he could have escaped, that his body suffers but his soul is glad, because he fears God.
settings.readers: 4 Maccabees, written later for Greek-speaking Jews, built a whole discourse on Eleazar's death to show that devout reason masters the passions (4 Maccabees 1:1; 5:1–7:23). That later book shows how this scene was read by Jews like the first readers of 2 Maccabees.
views: Christian readers have compared the words with Acts 5:41 and Matthew 5:11–12.
Scholars note the Greek contrast of body and soul, joined to the Jewish fear of God.

title: The Mother and Her Seven Sons
sum: Seven brothers and their mother are arrested and tortured to make them eat pork. The first, their spokesman, says they are ready to die rather than break their fathers' laws; the king has his tongue cut out, his scalp torn off, his hands and feet cut off, and orders him fried alive. One by one the others are tortured and killed, and each speaks before he dies: God will have pity on his servants; "the King of the world will raise us" (7:9); the third holds out his tongue and hands, hoping to receive them back from Heaven; for the king "there will be no resurrection to life" (7:14); God has not deserted his people; the king will not escape after fighting against God.

The mother watches all seven die in one day. In their ancestral tongue she tells them she did not form them in the womb; the Creator who did will give them back breath and life. The king offers the youngest wealth and a place among his Friends and asks the mother to persuade him. She leans over him, laughs at the tyrant, and urges him to look at the sky and earth that God made "not from things that were," and to accept death, so that she may receive him back with his brothers. The youngest gives the longest speech: they suffer for their own sins, God's anger is short, and he offers his body and life that in him and his brothers the Almighty's anger may stop. He dies, and last of all, the mother.
readings: The chapter is the most famous martyr story of the ancient Jewish world. It is built as a series of seven short speeches, then the mother's, then the youngest's long reply. Its theology is in the speeches: resurrection, creation, the justice of God, and the power of faithful death.

The king's presence, the order of tortures and the speeches make most historians read the story as a model tale, shaped to teach. But it may preserve the memory of real families who died in 167 BC, as 6:10–11 and 1 Maccabees 1:60–63 report.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads this chapter as an inspired witness to the resurrection of the body and to creation from nothing (Catechism 297 quotes the mother's words of 7:22–23, 28; Catechism 992 cites 7:9, 14, 29). The mother and her sons are honored as the Holy Maccabean Martyrs on 1 August. Whether their sufferings can help others, see the card below.
views.O: The Orthodox churches keep the Holy Maccabees on 1 August and call the mother Solomonia. John Chrysostom preached on them, and by Augustine's time a church in Antioch was dedicated to them. The Orthodox read the chapter as a witness to the resurrection and as the prelude to the Christian martyrs.
views.P: Protestants do not count the book as Scripture, but most read this chapter as a true witness to the faith of Jews before Christ: belief in the resurrection (Daniel 12:2) and creation by God alone. Many commentators think Hebrews 11:35 refers to these martyrs. Protestants reject any idea that the martyrs' deaths atone for others alongside Christ's.
views.H: Historians and scholars see in the chapter one of the earliest clear statements of bodily resurrection (with Daniel 12:2), and an early form of the idea that a martyr's death can end God's anger against a nation. They debate whether 7:28 teaches creation out of nothing, and trace the chapter's influence on 4 Maccabees, on Christian martyr acts and on rabbinic stories.
views.J: The rabbis knew a story of a mother and seven sons who would not bow to an idol, set in Roman times (Bavli Gittin 57b; Lamentations Rabbah on Lamentations 1:16). The second version stands in the midrash on Lamentations, the book read on the fast of Tisha b'Av, and in later Jewish tradition the mother is called Hannah. Jewish thought also drew on the martyrs for the idea of dying "for the sanctification of the Name."

deep.b:
This chapter says more about the resurrection than any other Jewish text before the New Testament. The second brother says, "the King of the world will raise us... to live again forever" (7:9). The third holds out his tongue and hands: "from him I hope to receive them back" (7:11). The fourth tells the king, "For you, though, there will be no resurrection to life" (7:14). The mother hopes to receive her sons back "in the mercy to come" (7:29). The hope is for a bodily rising, the same body given back, and it is the reward of those who die for God's laws.

Only Daniel 12:2 is as clear before it: "Many of those who sleep in the ground of dust will wake up, some to everlasting life, and some to disgrace, to everlasting abhorrence." The two books come from the same years. Within a century the Pharisees taught the resurrection, and the Sadducees denied it (Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8). Jesus' answer to the Sadducees, about seven brothers married to one woman (Mark 12:20–23), has reminded many readers of this chapter. On whether the dead are aware before the resurrection, see the card at 1 Enoch 102.

deep.h: "Not from things that were": creation out of nothing?
deep.b:
The mother's words in 7:28, that God made the sky and the earth ouk ex ontōn, "not from things that were," are the oldest Jewish text usually cited for creation out of nothing. The Vulgate translated ex nihilo; Origen, about AD 225, cited "the mother of the seven martyrs" for the teaching (On First Principles 2.1.5); and the Catholic Catechism quotes the verse (Catechism 297).

Many modern scholars think the verse says less than the later doctrine, which denies that any matter existed before God made the world. Gerhard May, in his history of the doctrine, finds in it only the idea that the world came into being by God's sovereign act; rejecting eternal matter, he says, lies outside the text's horizon, and Xenophon could speak of bringing children forth "from what is not" in an everyday sense. Jonathan Goldstein (1984) also denied that the verse teaches creation from nothing, and argued more widely that the doctrine arose later to defend bodily resurrection. David Winston (1986) disputed that wider thesis, and Goldstein partly withdrew it (1987). Paul Copan, against May, defends the older reading, and Barbara Schmitz, surveying the debate, finds the verse's concern to be God's sovereignty rather than a theory of first matter. Wisdom of Solomon, from a similar setting, says God made the world "out of formless matter" (Wisdom 11:17).

The mother's point is practical: the God who made all things, and makes each child, can make her son live again. The churches' answers on the doctrine are on the card below.

The story grew in many directions. 4 Maccabees, written in Greek probably in the first century AD, retells chapters 6–7 at length to prove that devout reason rules the passions, and calls the martyrs' death "a ransom for the sin of the nation" (4 Maccabees 17:21–22). Hebrews 11:35–36 almost certainly remembers them: "others were tortured, not accepting release, so that they might gain a better resurrection," with the rare words for the torture frame (6:19) and mockery (7:7).

Christians honored them as martyrs from the fourth century. Gregory of Nazianzus, John Chrysostom and Augustine preached on their feast; a shrine in Antioch claimed their relics; and the Orthodox and the Roman Martyrology keep them on 1 August. The rabbis told their own version, set under the Roman emperor, in which the mother tells her youngest to say to Abraham, "You bound one son on the altar; I bound seven" (Bavli Gittin 57b).

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:36; Deuteronomy 31:19–21; Daniel 12:2; Daniel 3:16–18; Genesis 1:1–2; Genesis 2:7; Psalm 139:13–16; Job 10:8–12; Isaiah 53:4–12; Psalm 44:22; Psalm 113:9; Hebrews 11:35–36; John 11:24–25; John 5:29; Mark 12:18–27; Acts 5:29; Acts 5:39; Romans 4:17; Hebrews 11:3

settings.by: the eldest brother, the family's spokesman
settings.when: 167 BC, at the start of the tortures
settings.why: To refuse the king's demand at once and declare the family ready to die rather than break the laws of their fathers.
settings.readers: The book's readers knew "the laws of our fathers" as the right Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings had granted to Jews (Josephus, Antiquities 12.142). The phrase made the martyrs' cause the readers' own: the ancestral law by which they lived in Greek cities.
views: The answer is a refusal to bargain: the king may ask, but they will not answer as he wishes.
Scholars note that each brother's words form a short confession, a pattern later martyr acts follow.

settings.when: 167 BC, during the first brother's death
settings.why: To strengthen each other to die bravely, recalling that in the Song of Moses God promises pity for his servants (Deuteronomy 32:36).
settings.readers: The readers read their Scriptures in Greek; the quotation follows the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:36. 4 Maccabees 18:18–19 has the mother remember that their father taught them the Song of Moses, so later Greek-speaking Jews pictured such families learning these words at home.
views: The Song promises that God will relent toward his servants: the persecution will end.
The Song also says Israel's sin brings punishment; the brothers accept both parts (7:18, 32–33).

settings.why: To mock the brother and offer him one last chance: eat, or be tortured limb by limb.
settings.readers: The test was pork, and Greek writers in Egypt mocked the Jews for it: Josephus answers the Alexandrian Apion, who complained that Jews do not eat pork (Against Apion 2.137). Readers in Alexandria knew this ridicule at first hand.
views: The question is the king's offer in its plainest form.
The writer calls it a cruel game (7:7, 10); Hebrews 11:36 may recall such mockings.

settings.why: To tell the king that he takes only this present life, and that the King of the world will raise those who die for his laws to life forever.
settings.readers: The readers lived after the resurrection hope of Daniel 12:2 had been written down. The book itself, in 12:43–45 and 14:46, shows the same hope shaping Judas's prayer and Razis's death, so it was part of the faith the writer expected his readers to share.
views: Most readers take the words of a bodily rising, as 7:11 makes plain.
Scholars note that the hope is for those who die for God's laws; the book is silent on the rest of the dead.

settings.why: To hold out his tongue and hands as gifts of Heaven he gives up for God's laws, hoping to receive them back.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt also wrote of the soul's survival in Greek terms: Wisdom of Solomon, probably from Alexandria, says "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God" and that "a perishable body weighs down the soul" (Wisdom 3:1; Wisdom 9:15). Against that background the third brother's hope for his own tongue and hands is pointed.
views: The hope is for the very limbs to be restored (compare 14:46).
Some Christian readers, with 1 Corinthians 15:35–44, think of a body raised but transformed.

settings.why: To choose death in the hope of being raised, and to tell the king he will have no resurrection to life.
settings.readers: By the readers' time Jews disputed the afterlife: Josephus places the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes already under Jonathan, about 145 BC (Antiquities 13.171–173), and says the Pharisees held that the wicked are punished forever while the Sadducees denied any life after death (Jewish War 2.163–165). The brother's "no resurrection to life" takes a side in a live question.
views: Some read the verse as denying the king any resurrection.
Others note the words "to life": the king may rise, but to judgment (Daniel 12:2; John 5:29).

settings.why: To tell the king that his power is mortal, that God has not deserted his people, and that God will punish him and his offspring.
settings.readers: Readers after 124 BC had seen the line of Antiochus IV end: his son Antiochus V was killed in 162 BC (1 Maccabees 7:2–4), and Alexander Balas, who claimed to be his son, was killed in 145 BC (1 Maccabees 10:1; 1 Maccabees 11:17). For them "you and your offspring" had come true.
views: The writer presents the words as fulfilled in chapter 9 and 14:2.
The words also comfort readers that God has not left his people (6:16).

settings.why: To say that the people suffer for their own sins, and that the king, who has set out to fight God, will not go free.
settings.readers: The writer's readers had been told in 6:12–17 that suffering was God's discipline. Here a martyr speaks the same lesson, which helped readers see their own history as sin, punishment and mercy.
views: The brother speaks for the nation, not for his own sins.
Readers of Acts hear Gamaliel's warning (Acts 5:39).

settings.to: each of her sons, in the ancestral language
settings.why: To encourage her sons to die by reminding them that God, not she, formed them in the womb, and that he will give them back breath and life.
settings.readers: The book's first letter, sent to the Jews of Egypt, prays to the "Lord God, maker of all things" (1:24), and Wisdom of Solomon, a Greek Jewish book probably from Alexandria, speaks of a child molded in the womb from seed and blood (Wisdom 7:1–2). Readers there were used to joining creation and the making of each child, as the mother does.
views: The argument runs from God's power as Creator to his power to raise.
Readers have long noted that the book gives the clearest statement of its faith to a woman.

settings.why: To win over the last son by promising on oath to make him rich, envied, a Friend of the king and a royal officer, if he leaves his ancestral ways.
settings.readers: Readers in Greek cities knew the court titles; 1 Maccabees shows such offers made to Mattathias (1 Maccabees 2:18). Some Jews in Egypt did rise high at the Ptolemaic court (Josephus, Against Apion 2.49), so the offer was a real temptation to readers too.
views: The king tries money where torture failed.
The offer of "Friend" was the highest honor a subject could have.

settings.to: her youngest son, in the ancestral language
settings.why: To seem to obey the king while urging her son to die: to look at the creation made "not from things that were" and accept death, so she may receive him back.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews in Egypt spoke about creation in more than one way: Wisdom of Solomon says God made the world "out of formless matter" (Wisdom 11:17). The mother's "not from things that were" stands beside that sentence in the same world of readers, and scholars still debate whether the two differ.
views: Origen and the Catechism take 7:28 as creation out of nothing (Origen, On First Principles 2.1.5; Catechism 297), and Paul Copan defends that reading.
May, Goldstein and others think the verse says only that God made the world by his own act, without deciding whether matter existed before; see the chapter's deep section.

settings.what: The youngest son's speech and prayer
settings.why: To refuse the king, declare that the people suffer for their sins and that God's anger is short, warn the king of judgment, and, with his brothers, call on God to stop his anger against the nation in their deaths.
settings.readers: The book's readers knew what followed: Judas gathered his men, and "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (8:5). The prayer's answer was part of the history they read. 4 Maccabees 17:21–22 shows that later Greek-speaking Jews understood the deaths as a ransom for the nation.
views: The martyrs' deaths end the wrath
Van Henten reads the martyrs as the nation's saviors: their deaths turn God's anger (8:5), as 4 Maccabees 17:21–22 later says outright.
Others stress that in Swete's text the brothers call on God "to stop" his anger (7:38): it is God who ends it. Venetus and the KJV, where the anger simply "may cease", lean the other way.

settings.what: The writer closes the martyr stories
settings.why: To end the account of the sacrificial meals and tortures, judging that what has been told is enough.
settings.readers: The summarizer promised to give readers ease and benefit (2:25). Stopping here, before the victories, marks the martyrs' deaths as the turning point of the story.
views: The writer marks the end of the persecution section.
Van Henten sees the martyrs' deaths as what turns the story from disaster to rescue.

traditions.q: The youngest brother calls on God to stop his anger in him and his brothers (7:37–38). Can the sufferings of faithful people help atone for others, or does only Christ's death atone? (Whether good works atone for sin is asked at Proverbs 16; whether the saints in heaven pray for us, at Revelation 5; whether sins can be cleansed after death, on the 2 Maccabees 12 card.)
views: They can share in Christ's one sacrifice, never add to it. Jesus "desires to associate with his redeeming sacrifice those who were to be its first beneficiaries" (Catechism 618), and the sick who suffer can "complete" in their flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for his body, the church (Catechism 1508, on Colossians 1:24). John Paul II taught that Christ's redemption is complete, yet "remains always open to all love expressed in human suffering" (Salvifici doloris 24). In the communion of saints "the holiness of one profits others" (Catechism 1475).

Only Christ's death atones, and the saints are honored without being trusted. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession denies that the merits of the saints are applied to others, "the merits of Christ alone are a propitiation for us", and honors the saints in three ways: thanks to God for them, the strengthening of faith by their example, and the imitation of their faith and virtues (article 21).

Only Christ's death atones, and no believer has merit to spare. Christ "by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself" fully satisfied the Father's justice (Westminster Confession 8.5), while even the most obedient "fall short of much which in duty they are bound to do" (16.4), so no one can do more than God requires for the benefit of others.

Only Christ's death atones: "The Offering of Christ once made is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction, for all the sins of the whole world", and "there is none other satisfaction for sin, but that alone" (Article 31). Works beyond God's commands, "works of supererogation", "cannot be taught without arrogancy and impiety" (Article 14).

traditions.q: The mother says God made the sky and the earth "not from things that were" (7:28). Did God create the world out of nothing, or shape it from matter that already existed?
views: Out of nothing, and 2 Maccabees itself is a witness. God "needs no pre-existent thing or any help in order to create"; Scripture bears witness to creation "out of nothing" as a truth full of hope, and the Catechism quotes the mother of the seven sons, 7:22–23 and 7:28, for it (Catechism 296–297). The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed God as the one who from nothing made both spiritual and bodily creatures.

Out of nothing, on the ground of the 66 books alone, since the Westminster Confession does not count 2 Maccabees among them (1.3). It pleased God "in the beginning, to create, or make of nothing, the world, and all things therein" (4.1), with Hebrews 11:3 among its proof texts.

From eternal matter. Joseph Smith taught in the King Follett discourse (1844) that the Hebrew word for create "does not mean to create out of nothing; it means to organize," and that God made the world from "chaotic matter, which is element," which has always existed. A revelation says that "the elements are eternal" (Doctrine and Covenants 93:33).
